steps.body:
Welcome back. You can store values and do math with them now. Today we deal with the thing that scares people off programming more than anything else: the wall of red error text.

Here is the reframe that changes everything. An error is not Python yelling at you. It is Python HELPING you. Every error message is a little map that tells you two things: what went wrong, and exactly where.

That wall of text is called a traceback. Read it from the BOTTOM up. The very last line is the important one: it names the type of error and gives a short message. Just above that, Python points at the exact line it tripped on. So the bottom line is what broke, and the line above is where. Once you read tracebacks instead of fearing them, you stop being stuck and start being a debugger. Nobody writes code without errors. The whole skill is reading them.

steps.prompt: Run this on purpose. It breaks. Read the bottom line of the traceback: it names the error and the line.
You run a program and the bottom line of the traceback says:  TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str.  In plain words, what is Python telling you?

steps.body:
Almost every error you hit for months will be one of five. Learn these five faces and you will recognize most trouble on sight.

NameError: you used a name Python has never seen. Usually a typo, or you forgot to create it.
TypeError: you tried to mix two kinds of values that do not go together, like adding text to a number.
SyntaxError: the code is not shaped like valid Python (a missing colon, an unclosed quote or bracket). Python cannot even begin to run it.
IndexError: you asked a list for a slot that is not there, like the 5th item of a 3-item list.
ValueError: the value is the right TYPE but the wrong CONTENT, like asking int() to read the word twenty, or the decimal "3.5".

That is the whole rogues gallery. Let us practice spotting them.

steps.prompt: Read this in your head. The list has three items (positions 0, 1, 2). Which error does the last line raise?

reviewForm.prompt: Asking a 3-item list for items[5] raises which error?
reviewForm.expected: IndexError, the position does not exist.

steps.prompt: int() can read a string of digits, but not a word. Which error does this raise?

reviewForm.prompt: int("twenty") raises which error? The value is a string (right type) but not readable as a number (wrong content).

steps.prompt: Run it in your head and you get a NameError: name 'sid' is not defined. Read that as a map: the name sid does not exist. Find the typo and fix it so the function returns the area of a square.
hints: The error names the culprit: sid. There is no box called sid.
You meant the parameter side. It is a one-letter typo.

reviewForm.prompt: NameError: name 'sid' is not defined. Fix the typo.

hiddenTests.message: the name should be side, not sid

steps.prompt: This raises TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str. Translation: you are gluing a number onto text. score is a number. Fix it so label_score(10) returns the string Score: 10.

hiddenTests.message: label_score(10) should return the string: Score: 10
check 0 too: it should read Score: 0

hints: You cannot add a number onto text. Turn the number into text first with str(), or use an f-string.
str(score) turns 10 into "10". Or write f"Score: {score}".

reviewForm.prompt: TypeError from gluing a number onto text. Fix it.

lessons.title: Off by One, and Breaking It on Purpose

steps.prompt: This is meant to return the THIRD item of a list. On a three-item list it raises IndexError: list index out of range. Remember that positions start at 0, so the third item lives at position 2, not 3. Fix it.

hiddenTests.message: the third item of [a, b, c] is c, which lives at position 2
the third item should be 30, at position 2, not position 3

hints: Positions start counting at 0, so item one is at 0, item two is at 1, item three is at 2.
items[3] is actually the fourth slot, which does not exist in a three-item list.

reviewForm.prompt: IndexError, off by one. The third item is at which position?

hiddenTests.message: positions start at 0, so the third item is items[2]

steps.prompt: The text here is a temperature like "36.6". Calling int() on it raises ValueError: invalid literal for int(). The value is a real number, just not a WHOLE one, so int() refuses it. The tool for decimals is float() (you met it in Module 2). Fix read_temp so it returns the decimal as a number.

hiddenTests.message: read_temp("98.4") should give 98.4, so it must handle any decimal

hints: int() only reads whole numbers. "36.6" has a decimal point.
The tool for decimals is float(), the same way int() is the tool for whole numbers.

reviewForm.prompt: ValueError: int() cannot read "36.6". Which converter reads decimals?

steps.prompt: Break something on purpose. In the scratch console, write a tiny line you KNOW will fail (misspell a name, or add a number to a word), run it, and read the traceback. Then, in a sentence or two, describe: which of the five errors did you get, and how did the bottom line of the traceback tell you exactly what and where? Making errors happen on demand is how you stop fearing them.

boss.name: The Debugging Gauntlet
boss.taunt: Five programs. Five bugs. One of each classic kind. Read the maps and fix them all.

terms.definition: The block of error text Python prints when something breaks. Read it bottom-up: the last line names the error and the line above points at where it happened.
You used a name Python has never seen. Usually a typo or a variable you forgot to create.
You tried to combine two kinds of values that do not mix, like adding a number onto text.
The code is not shaped like valid Python (a missing colon, an unclosed quote or bracket). Python cannot even start.
You asked a list for a position that does not exist, like the 5th item of a 3-item list. Positions start at 0.
The value is the right type but the wrong content, like asking int() to read the word twenty or the decimal "3.5".
